name: Quinine
route_note: oral tablets three times daily for 7 days, usually with doxycycline or clindamycin; IV infusion or IM injection where artesunate is unavailable
targets: Haem detoxification in the Plasmodium food vacuole
originator: Isolated from cinchona bark by Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou

discovery.by: Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou, Paris
discovery.note: Alkaloid purified from the bark of South American Cinchona trees, used against fevers since at least the 17th century.

tagline: The original antimalarial from cinchona bark, now a backup for severe malaria
summary: Quinine is an alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree and was the first effective chemical treatment for malaria. It has largely been replaced by artemisinin derivatives, but it remains an alternative for severe malaria when artesunate is not available and for uncomplicated malaria in some settings. Cinchonism and serious blood disorders limit its use; it is no longer recommended for leg cramps.
mechanism: Quinine acts on the blood stages of malaria parasites. Like other quinoline antimalarials it is thought to accumulate in the parasite's food vacuole and inhibit polymerisation of haem into haemozoin, so toxic haem builds up.

It also has effects on muscle membranes and sodium channels, which underlie its former use for cramps and its cardiac toxicity. Its stereoisomer quinidine was used as an antiarrhythmic and as IV antimalarial.
uses: Uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria (oral, with doxycycline, tetracycline or clindamycin)
Severe malaria when parenteral artesunate is unavailable
Malaria in the first trimester of pregnancy (with clindamycin; some guidelines)

history.title: Jesuit's bark
history.detail: By the 1630s cinchona bark from Peru is in use against fevers; Jesuits bring it to Europe in the following decades.

history.title: Isolation
history.detail: Pelletier and Caventou isolate quinine from cinchona bark in Paris.

history.title: Plantations
history.detail: Dutch and British efforts to cultivate cinchona in Java and India begin, eventually giving Java a near-monopoly on supply.

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Robert Woodward and William Doering report a formal total synthesis of quinine.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: Qualaquin becomes the first FDA-approved quinine product, for uncomplicated falciparum malaria.

history.title: Leg cramps ban
history.detail: The FDA orders unapproved quinine products off the market, citing serious and fatal adverse events with use for nocturnal leg cramps.

history.title: Replaced by artesunate
history.detail: The AQUAMAT trial leads WHO to prefer artesunate over quinine for severe malaria in children.

common: cinchonism (tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, nausea, visual disturbance)
serious: thrombocytopenia, haemolytic uraemic syndrome/TTP and disseminated intravascular coagulation
safety.boxed_warning: Use for nocturnal leg cramps may cause serious and life-threatening haematological reactions, including thrombocytopenia and HUS/TTP; not approved for that use (US label).

facts: Quinine is responsible for the bitter taste of tonic water, which contains much lower amounts than medicinal doses.
Its scarcity during the Second World War spurred programmes that produced chloroquine and other synthetic antimalarials.
